title: burst-windowed-batcher-inspection-notes
content:
Summary:

This is a working note for the burst-windowed batcher investigation — a lightweight scheduler variant we prototyped to handle brief, high-intensity microbursts without inflating average latency for stable traffic. The goal: reduce 99.9/99.99 tail spikes during 5--30s bursts while preserving throughput and keeping token cost per request close to baseline.

Motivation / Background:
- Continuous batching gives great throughput, but we still see tail spikes when short bursts of traffic arrive and the normal coalescer forms large, heterogeneous batches that block low-latency requests.
- Prior experiments (see RED-2718) looked at timeout annealing and urgency weights; this note explores a windowed-batcher that adaptively creates short-duration "burst windows" with aggressive small-batch preference and fast flush policy.
- We want something cheap to reason about and implement in the runtime (no heavy ML models).

Prototype design (burst-windowed batcher):
- On burst detection (queue growth rate threshold over X ms), allocate a temporary burst window for N ms.
- Within window: prefer forming batches with max_size_small (e.g., 8) and enforce low timeout (e.g., 2ms) for flush; demote large-batch formation for full-length requests.
- After window ends, fade back to default continuous-batcher via exponential cooldown.
- Fairness: give each service tier a virtual-deadline boost inside burst window to avoid starving low-priority traffic.

Key knobs we swept (matrix):
- burst_detection_rate_threshold: {0.5, 1.0, 2.0} reqs/ms over 50ms window
- window_duration_ms: {10, 25, 50}
- max_size_small: {4, 8, 16}
- small_batch_timeout_ms: {1, 2, 5}
- cooldown_tau_ms: {100, 250, 1000}
- fairness_boost: {none, light, aggressive}

Test harness and workloads used:
- Replay harness from production traces (sanitized): 6 replay snippets with 10--40s microbursts embedded in steady background traffic (baseline qps ~120).
- Synthetic microburst generator: spike shapes (single sharp spike, plateau, multi-peak).
- Model: Llama-2 13B quantized path used for latency-sensitive runs (kv-cache enabled), and a smaller 7B for cost-focused runs.
- Each run executed 3x to capture variance; we collected per-request microtraces, kernel occupancy, and scheduler event logs.

Primary metrics captured (per-run):
- p50/p95/p99/p99.9 latency (ms) end-to-end
- tokens/sec throughput and tokens/request cost estimate
- Batch size distribution (histogram) during burst vs baseline
- KV-cache hit/miss rate and average KV-cache prefill time
- Scheduler CPU/lock contention (sampled stacks)

Representative results (high-level):
- Best config: detection_rate 1.0 reqs/ms over 50ms, window_duration 25ms, max_size_small 8, small_batch_timeout 2ms, cooldown_tau 250ms, fairness_boost light.
  - p99.9 reduced by ~48% on sharp single spikes compared to baseline continuous-batcher.
  - p99 reduced by ~22%.
  - Throughput drop negligible (<1.5%), token cost delta +0.8%.
  - Batch size distribution shifted: median batch size in burst window = 7 (vs baseline 18).
- Aggressive small_batch_timeout (1ms) sometimes caused extra flushes that moved work to more expensive kernel paths (higher per-token GPU overhead) — observed small increase in scheduler CPU.
- Larger max_size_small (16) lost most benefit on p99.9 — batches still grew large quickly because sustained high arrival rate collapsed windows.
- Short window_duration (10ms) reduced tail less: detection lag meant some late arrivals joined large blocking batches.

Observed bottlenecks and traces:
- KV-cache prefill interaction: when requests include longer prefixes and require KV-cache prefill, small-batch tactic increased the fraction of requests that triggered separate prefill operations, increasing end-to-end latency for those requests. The effect is larger for models with expensive prefill (13B).
- Scheduler lock contention increased by ~15% in the best config vs baseline during the burst window (contention mostly around batch-formation queue head). Stack samples point to two hot funcs: queue_enqueue() and flush_coalesce().
- GPU kernel overhead: extra small batches increase kernel launch frequency. For quantized kernels that benefit from longer sequences, we observed lower GPU utilization in the burst window. Net throughput preserved because overall token volume unchanged but per-token overhead rose slightly.

Hypotheses / Interpretations:
1) Burst windows reduce queuing risk for short synthetic spikes, but must be tuned to avoid causing multiplier effects (more kernel launches, more prefill).
2) Fairness boost (light) helps avoid starving low-priority traffic; aggressive fairness reduced overall benefit because it constrained small-batch formation for high-priority traffic too much.
3) KV-cache-aware policy needed: detect prefill-heavy requests and treat them differently (either coalesce them preferentially into slightly larger batches or delay them by a fixed micro-delay).

Unresolved questions / experiments to run next:
- Implement a KV-prefill detector (cheap heuristic): if request.prefix_tokens > T, tag as prefill-heavy. Run A/B with policy: prefer coalescing prefill-heavy requests into size >= 12 even within burst windows. Measure p99/p99.9 and prefill duplicate counts.
- Try a hybrid policy that lets max_size_small vary with measured kernel occupancy (if GPU busy => smaller limit). This requires fast GPU occupancy sampling in the scheduler path; need perf analysis to ensure sampling cost is acceptable.
- Replace the simplistic cooldown with a token-based budget (burst budget that decays with processed tokens) to better handle back-to-back bursts.
- Test on longer plateau bursts (60--120s) to ensure we don't accidentally shift to a high-cost steady-state.

Action items (short-term):
- [Ravi] Add lightweight prefill detector and instrument prefill duplicates (JIRA RED-2794).
- [Lena] Profile queue lock hotspots and try lock-free enqueue micro-optimizations in a branch (PR referenced above).
- [Omar] Run plateau-burst replay suite and produce aggregated p99.9 comparison across configs (deadline 2025-03-12).
- [Ava] Draft proposal for KV-aware small-batch policy and estimate engineering effort.

Notes to self / loose ideas:
- Could try jittered window start times to de-synchronize multiple schedulers in the same node (avoid synchronized microflushes).
- Consider lightweight per-tenant burst budgets to avoid noisy-neighbour-induced windows.
- Keep a close eye on per-token GPU overhead; small wins in tail may be negated by 3--5% cost regressions at scale.

Appendix: quick checklist for reproducing the best run:
1) Checkout branch: serving-runtime/feature/burst-windowed (PR:812).
2) Use replay trace: s3://redwood-inference/benchmarks/burst-windowed/trace-A.json
3) Config: detect_rate=1.0, window_ms=25, max_small=8, timeout_small=2ms, cooldown_tau=250ms, fairness=light.
4) Run 3 repeats, collect microtraces and scheduler logs.

End of note.

---
This doc is a field inspection; will iterate into a formal playbook once the KV-prefill mitigation is explored.
